article.overview: A thermal management demonstrator is a test article or flight experiment that shows how a lunar system can keep its hardware within safe temperature limits. The Moon presents two thermal problems. During the roughly 14-day lunar night, equipment must be kept warm enough to survive, and during the lunar day, heat must still be rejected to space or the surface. Hardware such as variable conductance heat pipes [1], radiator shutters [3] and waste-heat transfer paths [2] address these needs. Thermal management is a class of technology rather than one standard instrument, so this article describes several documented examples. These range from a heat pipe flown in transit on the Peregrine Mission One lander [1] to a breadboard radiator shutter [3], a laboratory and thermal-vacuum demonstration of an ice-mining heat system [2], and a power-infrastructure concept with a passive thermal design [5]. A news report of a flown Chinese lander and rover surviving their first lunar night is also noted [6].
article.description:
The term covers passive and active hardware that moves heat through a lunar system. A variable conductance heat pipe (VCHP) is a heat pipe with a reservoir of non-condensable gas. The gas position changes how much of the condenser is active, so heat transfer falls when the heat sink is cold [1]. A radiator shutter covers a radiator with an aluminised film, changing how much of the radiator can see cold space or the lunar surface [3]. A waste-heat system carries heat from a power source into a drill or cold trap so that water ice can be sublimated and collected [2]. A passive thermal-storage design uses a large mass of phase-change material to absorb heat during high-dissipation periods and release it during cold survival periods [5].

Two quantities recur across the sources. The turndown ratio is the ratio of the heat-pipe conductance in its design (on) condition to its conductance in the low-power survival condition. The ACT ground test reported an estimated turndown ratio of 185:1 [1]. A 2013 NASA and ATK thermal switching system reported a switching ratio of 200 to 400 [4]. Survival power is the electrical heating needed to keep equipment above its minimum temperature when heat transfer is minimised. The ACT test reported 1 W for this condition in ground testing [1].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of these demonstrators is to show that thermal hardware can work reliably in lunar or lunar-like conditions before it is relied on for a mission. The sources describe several intended applications. The Peregrine heat pipe was intended to support a lunar lander, operating during transit and, if the landing had succeeded, on the lunar surface [1]. The 2013 NASA and ATK architecture was developed for a small robotic lunar lander and for other variable heat rejection missions [4]. The ESA-funded shutter was intended for lunar radiators, including applications where limiting dissipation helps lunar-night survival, such as ESA Argonaut applications [3]. The ice-mining system was intended for resource extraction in permanently shadowed regions [2]. TEMPEST is a concept for transmitting power into permanently shadowed regions, with thermal management as a supporting function [5]. These are intended applications rather than demonstrated operational results.
article.operating_principle:
Variable conductance heat pipes work by passively changing how much of the condenser is available to the working fluid [1]. In the cold-reservoir design, the non-condensable gas reservoir follows the heat-sink temperature. As the sink gets colder, the gas expands and blocks more of the condenser, which limits heat loss from the source. The ICES paper states that a cold-biased reservoir typically needs electrical heating of 1-2 W for the whole 14-day lunar night to push the gas front close to the evaporator [1]. The hot-reservoir design, used for the Peregrine unit, places the reservoir close to the evaporator so that it follows the heat-source temperature. Its hybrid wick combines a 3D-printed porous evaporator with grooved sections for microgravity operation [1].

The radiator shutter changes the view factor of the radiator. A stepper motor drives tensioned belts and a spreader bar that draw the film over the radiator. The paper reports that the film keeps dust away from the bearings and tribological surfaces [3]. The ice-mining system uses a VCHP cold-trap tank. The paper reports demonstrations of an ice collection mode and an ice removal mode using this control, cooled by liquid-nitrogen cold plates [2]. The exact control sequence is shown in figures that were not reviewed for this article. The TEMPEST design uses a passive multi-component thermal system with phase-change material to absorb heat from component inefficiencies and release it slowly during an 18-hour cold cycle [5].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar hardware must survive long cold nights while still rejecting heat during the day, and every watt used for survival heating is power that a lander, rover or power system must generate and store. The sources argue that passive or variable heat transfer can reduce survival-heater power and allow smaller radiators [1][3][4]. This matters for missions that depend on limited battery and solar power. The Peregrine flight test is the strongest evidence in this article, because it recorded thermal operation on a real spacecraft in transit [1]. The other examples are ground, vacuum or concept results, so their importance lies in showing feasibility and identifying design problems rather than proving lunar performance.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a thermal management demonstrator. The examples below use different fluids, sizes, control methods and test conditions, and they are at very different stages of development. Their values should not be compared directly unless the source states that they refer to the same test configuration.

examples.name: Non-integrated hot-reservoir VCHP with hybrid wick (ACT, NASA Marshall and Astrobotic)
examples.type: Flight-tested heat pipe on a lander
examples.status: Flown on Peregrine Mission One. The paper reports thermal testing during flight in microgravity transit. No lunar surface operation was reported, because the lander did not complete a landing [1].
key_specifications: Aluminium-ammonia heat pipe with argon as the non-condensable gas [1].
Lengths: evaporator 10.2 cm, adiabatic section 10.2 cm, condenser 17.8 cm [1].
Total mass: 0.347 kg, including the aluminium plate and Ultem-1000 legs [1].

Heaters: a 30 W reservoir heater and a 30 W evaporator heater were used in the flight tests; the paper states the 30 W evaporator heater was half the total applied power in the thermal control test [1].
ACT ground test: conductance of 2.93 W/°C at the design condition and 0.0158 W/°C at the low-power survival condition, giving an estimated turndown ratio of 185:1 [1].
ACT ground test: with a -100 °C chiller sink and 1 W input, the evaporator settled at -37 °C [1].
Flight thermal control test: the heat-sink panel stayed between -17 °C and +2 °C, and the unit reached a reasonable steady state with the 30 W evaporator heater [1].
Flight reliability test: constant 30 W evaporator power for 138,300 s (38 h 25 min), with temperatures reported as constant [1].
Flight anomaly: one thermistor was permanently damaged during purge heating; the paper states this did not prevent the test [1].
Maturity: the authors state that the flight results raised the device to TRL 8 [1].

examples.name: Lunar Thermal Shutter, dust-resilient radiator cover (ESA-funded; ESR Space, Almatech, Spacemech)
examples.status: Breadboard tested by ESR Space. The paper states the TRL was raised to 4 by the end of the programme, from an original target of TRL 3. No mission was allocated. A flight version is described, but the test campaign reported refers to the breadboard [3].
key_specifications: Frame: 710 mm by 410 mm [3].
Drive: stepper motor, stainless steel drive belts, spreader bar and aluminised film stored on a spool [3].
Baseline radiator: 0.6 m by 0.36 m (0.216 m²) [3].
Operating range: -150 °C to +70 °C; survival up to +120 °C [3].
Design mass budget: 9 kg per square metre of radiator area. A measured mass was not identified in the reviewed text [3].
Magnetic coupling mass: below 80 g [3].
Thermal tests: radiator heat emission varied from 6.3 W to 55.6 W (ambient case) and from 11.7 W to 73.9 W (cold case) between the closed and open positions [3].

Dust: a coarse test in the University of Glasgow dirty-vacuum facility with LHS-1 simulant. The mechanism operated normally after several dust exposures, and dust was prevented from entering the protected tribological surfaces [3].

Life: a lower-level life assessment of 2000 open/close cycles (about 20% of the ECSS-factored lifetime). The breadboard achieved 1.44 million revolutions with no apparent degradation; a fully factored life requires 7.2 million cycles [3].

Low temperature: at -150 °C non-operational, a functional test showed belt slipping and spreader bar misalignment. The paper states that performance met requirements in all aspects except the low operational temperature [3].

examples.name: Waste-heat ice collection and extraction system with VCHP cold trap (ACT and Honeybee Robotics)
examples.type: Laboratory and thermal-vacuum demonstration; rover concept
examples.status: Demonstrated at lab scale and in relevant thermal-vacuum conditions. The authors give TRL 6 for the waste-heat ice drill. Not flown [2].
key_specifications: Thermal corer: SS316 sub-scale prototype with an inside diameter of 5 cm and a length of 17.3 cm, with integrated minichannels [2].
Test regolith: LHS-1 simulant with 5% water ice by mass [2].
Extraction: 13 g of ice extracted in the corer test, with about 60% recovery. In thermal-vacuum testing, recovery reached up to 18.2%, reduced by simulant carried over with the ice [2].
Cold trap: VCHP cold-trap tank with 10 heat pipes in three rows, with condensers cooled by liquid-nitrogen cold plates. Ice collection and ice removal modes were demonstrated [2].
Sizing (analysis, not test): each rover 115 kg; eight rovers estimated for the 2.78 kg/h target; about 24.3 kWh per 24-hour day [2].

examples.name: Passive thermal management for TEMPEST power-transfer infrastructure (Michigan Tech)
examples.type: Concept with reported tests; prototype status not stated
examples.status: The abstract reports a passive thermal design for permanently shadowed region operation and cryogenic tether testing. It does not state whether the thermal system is a prototype, a flight unit or a concept [5].
key_specifications: Transmission: about 3 km at 700 V DC between upstream TEMPEST, an aluminium tether and downstream TEMPEST with energy storage [5].
Thermal design: passive system with a large mass of phase-change material. The abstract does not state the mass or the amount of phase-change material [5].
Mission profile: 6 hours of high power dissipation followed by 18 hours of cold survival [5].
Tests: cryogenic tether testing characterised transient behaviour and communication characteristics [5].

examples.name: Serial VCHP and loop-heat-pipe thermal switching system (ATK and NASA Marshall, 2013)
examples.status: Tested. The abstract states the single-VCHP, single-LHP system was developed for a small robotic lunar lander and is applicable to other variable heat rejection missions. No flight is stated [4].
key_specifications: Architecture: serial linkage of hot-side VCHPs and cold-side loop heat pipes (LHPs) [4].
Tested configuration: one VCHP and one LHP [4].
Results: ON conductance of 2-4 W/K, OFF conductance of 0.01 W/K and an end-to-end switching ratio of 200-400 [4].
The ON test was run with a 60-70% gas-blocked VCHP condenser [4].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions vary widely. The Peregrine VCHP had evaporator, adiabatic and condenser lengths of 10.2 cm, 10.2 cm and 17.8 cm [1]. The ESA shutter frame measured 710 mm by 410 mm and was designed around a baseline radiator of 0.6 m by 0.36 m [3]. The ice-mining thermal corer was a sub-scale prototype with an inside diameter of 5 cm and a length of 17.3 cm [2]. The diameter of the Peregrine VCHP, and overall dimensions for the TEMPEST and 2013 NASA and ATK hardware, are not given in the text reviewed here.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Peregrine VCHP had a total mass of 0.347 kg, including its aluminium plate and low-conductivity legs [1]. The ESA shutter has a design mass budget of 9 kg per square metre of radiator area, and its magnetic coupling is stated to weigh less than 80 g [3]. A measured total mass for the shutter was not identified in the sections reviewed. The ice-mining analysis uses an assumed rover mass of 115 kg for sizing. This is an estimate, not a measured flight mass [2]. The other examples report no mass in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power requirements depend on the control method. The Peregrine tests used 30 W heaters. In ACT ground testing, a -100 °C chiller sink with 1 W of input held the evaporator at -37 °C, which the paper compares with a typical electronics survival temperature of about -40 °C [1]. The ESA radiator's heat emission varied from 6.3 W to 55.6 W between closed and open positions in the ambient case, and from 11.7 W to 73.9 W in the cold case [3]. The ice-mining sizing assumes one MMRTG per rover, giving 110 W electrical and 2000 W thermal power, and 100 W per corer at 1 mm/s traverse. These are design assumptions [2]. The TEMPEST mission profile is 6 hours of high power dissipation followed by 18 hours of cold survival, with no numerical power values in the abstract [5].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The sources describe several environments. The ICES paper refers to the lunar night, which lasts 14 days, as an extreme cold environment at about 100 K [1]. The ICES ground testing used a chiller sink as low as -100 °C, and the flight heat-sink panel stayed between -17 °C and +2 °C during the thermal control test [1]. The ESA shutter is specified for operation from -150 °C to +70 °C and survival up to +120 °C, and its tests used a vacuum chamber and a dirty-vacuum dust facility with LHS-1 simulant [3]. The ice-mining system is described for permanently shadowed regions with pressures below 1e-10 Torr and temperatures of 40 K to 80 K [2]. Launch loads were addressed by vibration testing for the Peregrine heat pipe at NASA Marshall [1]. The ESA paper states that its vibration and launch-load performance was not verified by test [3].
article.limitations: Most examples are breadboards, laboratory tests or concepts. Only the Peregrine heat pipe has reported in-flight thermal data, and that flight was a transit test with no landing [1]. Its reliability run lasted 38 hours in microgravity transit, not through a full lunar night [1]. Results from different hardware use different fluids, sizes, sink conditions and test definitions, so they cannot be ranked against each other. ACT's -100 °C ground chiller sink is a test condition, not a lunar condition [1]. The ESA shutter did not meet its low operational temperature requirement, and its lubricant lifetime is not verified [3]. The ice-mining paper identifies room for improvement in corer length and drill size, and its recovery figures are laboratory values [2].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Thermal management hardware is usually transported as part of a lander, rover or radiator assembly rather than as a stand-alone instrument. The examples differ. A heat pipe was mounted on a lander panel and flown [1]. A radiator mechanism is intended for a radiator surface [3]. A rover-mounted ice system exists at concept and laboratory stage [2], and a power-infrastructure concept is described [5]. Apart from the Peregrine example, none of these sources identifies a verified lunar lander or rover interface, so compatibility with other vehicles is not assessed here.
transportation_process: Integrate the heat pipe, heaters and thermocouples on an aluminium plate offset from the lander enclosure panel by low-conductivity legs, as done for the Peregrine unit [1].
Mount the condenser directly to the lander enclosure panel, which served as the heat sink [1].

Complete pre-flight testing: benchtop, vibration and thermal-vacuum testing at NASA Marshall, followed by a protoflight plan with test temperatures 10 °C above and below the allowable flight temperature range [1].
Launch on the maiden flight of the United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket, carrying Peregrine Mission One [1].

Cruise and lunar transfer: about two hours after launch a propulsion anomaly prevented the planned lunar landing. The mission was re-tasked to gather propulsion data and to provide power and communications to payloads. The lander later performed a controlled re-entry after travelling more than 535,000 miles over ten days [1].
In-flight operation: the heat pipe was tested in microgravity during transit, with data recorded through the mission's communication passes, including a short signal loss between ground stations [1].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Peregrine heat pipe was not deployed. It was fixed to the lander panel and tested in place [1]. The radiator shutter is intended as a fixed radiator cover that opens and closes under motor drive [3]. The ice-mining corer is described as a drill whose heat is supplied by a rover power source [2]. The TEMPEST design is described as a stationary infrastructure system [5]. None of the sources describes a verified lunar-surface deployment of these demonstrators.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Peregrine Mission One flight is the only example in this article with reported in-flight thermal data [1]. The Chang'e-4 lander and Yutu-2 rover are reported to have survived their first lunar night, but their transport and deployment details were not retrieved for this article [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The Peregrine heat pipe was designed for that lander and was integrated there [1]. For the radiator shutter, the paper states that no mission was allocated and that the design is scalable to different radiator sizes [3]. For the ice-mining rover system, the sizing uses assumed MMRTG and rover values that are not matched to a specific rover [2]. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted beyond the Peregrine example.

article.historical_significance: The Peregrine flight is the only flight-test thermal dataset in this article. The authors report that a previous integrated version of the heat pipe failed during 2017 testing at the International Space Station, and that the flight results for the non-integrated hybrid-wick design raised its TRL to 8 [1]. The 2013 ATK and NASA Marshall paper described a serial hot-side VCHP and cold-side LHP switching architecture aimed at small robotic lunar landers [4]. The ESA-funded shutter shows that a dust-resilient radiator cover can be built and tested, while its low-temperature failure and unverified lubricant lifetime show that the work is still at breadboard stage [3]. A news headline reports that the Chang'e-4 lander and Yutu-2 rover survived their first lunar night on the far side. This is a practical demonstration of thermal survival, although the heating technology used is not verified in this article [6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Several items remain uncertain. (1) The Peregrine flight facts come from the ICES paper text. Its figures, and the Peregrine Mission One post-mission report cited in that paper, were not inspected [1]. (2) The TEMPEST abstract does not state whether its thermal system is a prototype or a concept [5]. (3) The ESA paper describes a flight version, but the test campaign it reports refers to the breadboard [3]. (4) The Chang'e-4 heating technology is not verified. Secondary coverage conflicts on whether radioisotope heater units or generators were used [6]. (5) Values were read from text extracts of the ICES, TFAWS and ESA papers, and figure values were not checked. (6) A search summary attributed a 26-architecture ranking to a JHU/APL analysis. The NTRS abstract does not contain that ranking [4], so it is not used. (7) No verified direct image asset was identified, so no images are included.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are present, so no image URLs are recorded.

data_quality_notes: No direct image asset URL was verified for this payload. The images arrays are empty and no image placements are recorded.
The ESA paper's conference attribution (ESMATS 2025) is taken from the file name, not from the extracted text.
The three PDFs returned binary content from WebFetch. Their text was extracted locally with pdftotext. Figures were not inspected.

The Chang'e-4 heating technology is unresolved. Two SpaceNews fetch attempts failed with a connection reset, and search snippets conflict (radioisotope heater units versus a radioisotope thermoelectric generator). No specification from that example is used.
The search-summary claim of a JHU/APL ranking of 26 thermal switching architectures is not supported by the NTRS abstract [4] and is excluded.
Peregrine facts come from the ICES-2025-419 paper text. The Peregrine Mission One post-mission report cited in that paper was not opened.
TFAWS sizing values (rover mass, MMRTG power, corer power, 5% ice fraction) are assumptions stated in the paper, not verified mission values.
